text: Identify the transition function of an NFA with ε-moves.
author: Sample
explanation: An ε-NFA may move on a symbol or on ε, and may go to any set of states.

text: Explain whether this is true: the DFA produced by subset construction never has more than 2^n states, where n is the number of NFA states.
author: Sample
explanation: Each DFA state is a subset of the n NFA states.

text: Describe why the ε-closure must be taken after every move in subset construction.
author: Sample
model: After reading a symbol, the NFA may immediately follow ε-moves without consuming input, so every state reachable by ε from the move result is also active. Without the closure the DFA would miss those states and could reject strings the NFA accepts.

text: Compute ε-closure(q1) for the ε-NFA below.
author: Sample
src:
start: q0
final: q3
q0,a = q1
q1,ε = q2
q2,ε = q3
q3,b = q1
q2,a = q0

text: Trace the ε-NFA for a*b*c* on each string and decide whether it is accepted.
author: Sample
src:
start: q0
final: q2
q0,a = q0
q0,ε = q1
q1,b = q1
q1,ε = q2
q2,c = q2

text: Determine the number of states in the DFA obtained by subset construction from this NFA (third symbol from the end is a).
author: Sample
src:
start: q0
final: q3
q0,a = q0,q1
q0,b = q0
q1,a = q2
q1,b = q2
q2,a = q3
q2,b = q3

text: Justify or refute: if two DFAs have the same number of states and the same set of final states, they accept the same language.
author: Sample
explanation: Equal size says nothing about the transitions. For example, two 2-state DFAs over {a} can accept even-length and odd-length strings respectively; only a language-equivalence check (or a distinguishing string) settles it.

text: Construct an equivalent DFA for the ε-NFA of (a|b)*abb (Thompson form). Show the ε-closure used for every new state.
author: Sample

text: Design a DFA over {0,1} that accepts binary strings containing the substring 101.
author: Sample
reference:
start: A
final: D
A,0=A
A,1=B
B,0=C
B,1=B
C,0=A
C,1=D
D,0=D
D,1=D
